ru: взвинчивать цену, взвинтить цену; набавлять ставку, набавить ставку
separable: separable — *bid up the price*, and with a pronoun it must split, *bid it up*
gloss: To push the price of something higher by making one offer after another for it.
examples: Collectors are *bidding up* anything that comes out of that studio.
Two rival funds *bid* the stock *up* forty percent in a single week.
Rumors of a shortage have *bid up* the price of copper.
contrast: The auction verb never changes: *bid → bid → bid*. Only the *-ing* doubles the d — *bidding up*.

ru: нагрянуть, заявиться; внезапно приезжать, внезапно приехать
separable: inseparable — *blow into town*, never ✗ *blow town into*
gloss: To arrive somewhere suddenly and without warning.
examples: He *blows into* town twice a year and expects everyone to drop everything.
She *blew into* the office an hour late, still holding her coat.
A cousin I had never met had *blown into* town the night before.
contrast: *Blew* in the past, *blown* in the participle — never ✗ *blowed into*.

sense: carry something to where someone is
ru: приносить, принести; привозить, привезти; приводить, привести (к кому-л.)
separable: separable — *bring over a chair*, and with a pronoun it must split, *bring it over*
gloss: To carry or take someone or something to the place where the other person is.
examples: *Bring over* whatever you were planning to cook.
She *brought* her new boyfriend *over* on Sunday.
They have *brought over* half their furniture already.

ru: переманивать, переманить; склонять на свою сторону, склонить на свою сторону
separable: separable — *bring over the undecided voters*, and with a pronoun it must split, *bring them over*
gloss: To persuade someone to accept your opinion or join your side.
examples: Two more speeches might *bring over* the delegates who are still undecided.
The pay offer *brought* three of the holdouts *over*.
By Friday he had *brought over* even his loudest critics.

separable: inseparable — *climb down the ladder*, never ✗ *climb the ladder down*
transitivity: both — intransitive (*climb down slowly*), transitive (*climb down the ladder*)
gloss: To move down from a high place, holding on with your hands and feet.
examples: Hold the rails while you *climb down*.
He *climbed down* the fire escape in his socks.
She was *climbing down* from the hayloft when the ladder slipped.
contrast: The b is silent in every form: *climb*, *climbed*, *climbing* — KLYM, KLYMD, KLY-ming.

ru: отступать, отступить (от требований); идти на попятную, пойти на попятную
separable: no object — what is given up arrives through *from*: *climb down from that demand*
gloss: To admit you were wrong and give up a demand or a claim you had insisted on.
examples: Neither side wants to *climb down* first.
The company *climbed down* and paid the refunds.
They have *climbed down* from every threat they made.
contrast: American English says *back down* more often; *climb down* is the same retreat, seen from the position the speaker had climbed to.

ru: выходить, выйти (из чего-л.); получаться, получиться в результате
separable: inseparable — *come of the meeting*, never ✗ *come the meeting of*
gloss: To be the result of something.
examples: Nothing good *comes of* arguing with him.
Whatever *came of* that job offer in Denver?
Nothing has *come of* the complaint we filed.
contrast: *Come* is its own participle: *come → came → come*. ✗ *has came of*.

ru: сливать, слить; отводить, отвести (жидкость); откачивать, откачать
separable: separable — *draw off the liquid*, and with a pronoun it must split, *draw it off*
gloss: To remove liquid from a container or from the body by letting it flow out.
examples: *Draw off* the fat before you make the gravy.
The surgeon *drew* a liter of fluid *off* the lung.
Once the water has been *drawn off*, the tank can be scrubbed.
contrast: *Drew* in the past, *drawn* in the participle — never ✗ *drawed off*.

ru: убывать, убыть; таять, растаять (о поддержке); сходить на нет, сойти на нет
separable: no object — *support fell away*, never ✗ *fall the support away*
gloss: To become steadily fewer, weaker, or less until almost nothing is left.
examples: Attendance always *falls away* after the holidays.
Her support in the polls *fell away* week by week.
By March most of the volunteers had *fallen away*.

ru: круто спускаться, круто уходить вниз (о местности)
separable: no object — *the hillside falls away*, never ✗ *fall the hillside away*
gloss: Of ground, to slope sharply downward from where you are standing.
examples: Behind the cabin the hillside *falls away* into a ravine.
The path *fell away* so steeply that we went down on all fours.
We stood where the ground had *fallen away* to a beach two hundred feet below.

separable: inseparable — *fall over the cord*, never ✗ *fall the cord over*
transitivity: both — intransitive (*the lamp fell over*), transitive (*he fell over the cord*)
gloss: To topple from an upright position to the ground.
examples: The vase *fell over* when the door slammed.
Careful — that stack of books is going to *fall over*.
She had *fallen over* twice on the ice before she gave up.

ru: выпадать на долю, выпасть на долю; доставаться, достаться (об обязанности)
separable: inseparable — *it fell to me*, never ✗ *fall me to*
gloss: To become someone's duty or responsibility, usually because no one else will do it.
examples: Delivering bad news always *falls to* the manager.
It *fell to* me to tell the family.
Every unpleasant chore in this office has *fallen to* her.
contrast: Usually launched by a dummy *it*: *It fell to me to tell them*, not ✗ *To tell them fell to me*.

ru: передвигаться, перемещаться (особ. с трудом); выходить из дома
separable: no object — *get about on crutches*, never ✗ *get the crutches about*
gloss: To move from place to place, especially when age or injury makes it hard.
examples: At ninety she still *gets about* without a cane.
After the surgery he *got about* on crutches for a month.
She has *gotten about* much better since the new knee.
contrast: American English uses *gotten* for the participle (*has gotten about*); British English says *got about*. Americans also more often say *get around*.

ru: переходить, перейти (к теме); заговаривать, заговорить (о чём-л.)
separable: inseparable — *get onto politics*, never ✗ *get politics onto*
gloss: To start talking about a particular subject, often by drifting there.
examples: Whatever you do, don't *get onto* the subject of his divorce.
Somehow we *got onto* the war, and dinner was ruined.
Once he has *gotten onto* baseball, there is no stopping him.

sense: find out what someone is doing
ru: выходить на след, выйти на след; раскусить, разоблачить
separable: inseparable — *get onto the scheme*, never ✗ *get the scheme onto*
gloss: To find out about someone's secret or dishonest activity.
examples: It takes the auditors years to *get onto* a scheme like that.
The police *got onto* him through a tip from a neighbor.
By then the IRS had *gotten onto* the whole operation.
contrast: The t doubles in *getting onto*, and the American participle is *gotten*, not *got*.

separable: inseparable — *get round the rule*, never ✗ *get the rule round*
gloss: To find a way past a rule, an obstacle, or a difficulty without meeting it head-on.
examples: There is no way to *get round* the residency requirement.
They *got round* the ban by renaming the product.
Every firm in town has *gotten round* that tax somehow.
contrast: Americans normally write *get around*; *get round* is the British form of the same verb. The American participle is *gotten round*, the British *got round*.

ru: сочетаться, подходить друг к другу; гармонировать
separable: no object — *the colors go together*, never ✗ *go the colors together*
gloss: To look, taste, or work well in combination.
examples: Those two colors do not *go together*.
Nobody thought red wine and fish *went together* until that dinner.
Hard work and luck have always *gone together* in his telling of it.
contrast: The third person adds *-es*, the past is *went* and the participle *gone*: ✗ *has went together*.

separable: inseparable — *hang about the station*, never ✗ *hang the station about*
transitivity: both — intransitive (*stop hanging about*), transitive (*hang about the lobby*)
gloss: To stay in a place doing nothing in particular.
examples: Teenagers *hang about* the parking lot until the store closes.
We *hung about* for an hour and then gave up.
He has *hung about* that bar every night since he lost the job.
contrast: *Hang* meaning 'linger' is *hung*, never *hanged* — *hanged* belongs to executions. The everyday American wording is *hang around*.

separable: separable — *hold in your anger*, and with a pronoun it must split, *hold it in*
gloss: To keep a feeling from showing or escaping.
examples: Don't *hold in* your anger until it explodes.
She *held* her tears *in* until the door closed behind her.
He has *held in* so much resentment that it comes out sideways.
